spec.title: PROP-066 — Remap: replaceable artifact sources for closed networks, shared as packages

status.comment: Drafted 2026-10-31 on the owner's request; awaiting the owner's reading before implementation.

p.purpose: A vibe installation must work where the public hosts are unreachable, filtered, or forbidden by policy: no internet, a corporate network that allows one artifact store, a security team that names the only places bytes may come from. Every artifact vibe fetches gets a replaceable source, the replacement is declared once as data, and the declaration travels between people as an ordinary package. The failure this avoids is the one the owner met in NixOS: everything nailed to one public host, with no layer in between to point elsewhere.

p.principle: Identity is content, location is a replaceable detail. Everything vibe downloads already carries a hash (`vibe.lock` `content_hash`, `sha256` of application inputs, the publisher's digest in `DISTRIBUTIONS.json`, `content_hash` of embedded sources). A remap changes only where bytes are looked for; the bytes are verified against the same hash as before, so a remap can make a fetch fail or succeed but never change what is installed. Different bytes need a new capture and review, never a fallback that accepts them (`campaigns/next` R-027).

p.row: A remap is one `[[remap]]` row with three parts. **What** it matches, exactly one of: `sha256 = "<hex>"` (any artifact declared with that digest, whatever its URL); `package = "<group>/<name>[@<req>]"` (the registry package, its index entries and its embedded sources); `registry = "<name>"` (every URL a declared registry resolves to, including its index and raw-file endpoints); `prefix = "<url prefix>"` (every URL starting with it, the host rewrite). **With** what, exactly one of: `url = "…"` (an `https://`, `http://`, `file://` or git URL; for `prefix` the matched prefix is replaced by it, for the other keys it is the whole new location), `path = "…"` (a local file or directory; a directory is searched as `<path>/<sha256>/<filename>` the way the application download cache is laid out), or `deny = true` (the fetch is refused before any connection, naming the row). **Where** it applies, optional: `scope = { package = "…" }` or `scope = { package = "…", step = "ID" }` limits a row to the installation of one application package or one of its steps. Every row may carry `reason`, shown by `explain` and in refusals.

p.precedence: When several rows match one fetch the most specific key wins: `sha256`, then `package`, then `registry`, then `prefix` (the longest prefix among prefixes). A scoped row beats an unscoped row of the same key. Among equally specific rows the one from the higher layer of `#layers` wins, and inside one layer the later row. `vibe remap explain <url|sha256>` prints every matching row in winning order with its set and layer, so a surprising choice is one command away.

p.layers: Rows come from four layers, lowest first: remap packages installed in the user home (`vibe install -g org.corp/intranet`, `#package`); remap packages the project requires in `vibe.toml` (`[requires.remaps]`, resolved and locked like any dependency so every clone of the project gets the same set); local rows in `.vibe/settings.local.toml` and `~/.vibe/settings.toml` (`[[remap]]` tables, for one developer's machine); and the invocation, `--remap <file.toml>` (repeatable) or `VIBE_REMAP=<file>[,<file>]`. The existing registry `[[mirror]]` and `[[override]]` tables of PROP-002 stay as they are and are read as rows of the local layer (`registry = …` and `package = …` respectively), so nothing a user wrote stops working.

p.package: A remap package is a vibepack whose manifest declares `[package] kind = "remap"` and carries `[[remap]]` rows plus an optional `[policy]` table. It is versioned, content-hashed, published to any registry (an internal one included), installed with `vibe install -g` into the user home or required by a project, listed by `vibe list -g`, and removable like any package. It carries nothing executable. Several installed packages are read in their install order unless a package declares `priority = N` (higher wins among packages). `vibe remap disable|enable <package>` switches an installed package off and on without removing it; the switch lives in the user home, never in the package. This is how a colleague's or an architect's list reaches a team: publish it, require it, or hand it over on a disk.

p.policy: `[policy] unmatched = "allow" | "deny"` in a remap package or a local layer: with `deny`, any fetch no row matches is refused before a connection, naming the URL, the hash and the sets consulted. The strictest policy of all active layers applies. `vibe remap test` walks a project's or a home's declared artifacts (lock entries, application inputs of installed packages, the distribution manifest) and reports which row each one resolves to and whether the target answers a `HEAD`, without downloading, so a policy can be checked before it bites.

p.locator: One resolution point in `vibe-core` (`Locator`) is the only way a crate turns a declared source into the places to try. Its input is the artifact's identity (kind, declared URL or git locator, digest when declared, the package and step it belongs to); its output is the ordered candidate list with the winning row attached, or a `deny` refusal. Every fetch path adopts it: registry clones, redirects and git-source dependencies (PROP-002), the index and raw-file endpoints (PROP-005; the hardcoded `raw.githubusercontent.com` and `gitverse.ru` table becomes the default rows), embedded sources (PROP-021; the cache key becomes the content hash so the same bytes from another host hit), application inputs of `sources`, `archive` and `native` steps (PROP-059, PROP-065; `archive` and `native` inputs gain the same `<sha256>` cross-run cache `sources` have), `vibe self` distributions (PROP-019: the release base and the `DISTRIBUTIONS.json` location become remappable and the check that refused a non-GitHub base is dropped; the source-install mirror list accepts a remapped clone URL), the documentation shell (PROP-057), and the install scripts (`VIBEVM_RELEASE_ORIGIN` honoured, not only declared). The one `[proxy]` table (`https`, `http`, `no_proxy`) in settings reaches reqwest and child `git` through the same point.

p.not-covered: What a recipe script does on its own (`curl`, `git clone`, `pip install` inside a `recipe` step) is outside vibe's fetches and outside this PROP. Such a step declares `needs = "network"` (PROP-065), and under a `deny` policy the plan marks it `needs network, not remappable` so the reader sees it before the build starts. The recommended package shape in a closed network is to declare such downloads as `[[sources]]` inputs with digests, which this PROP then covers.

p.provenance: Where bytes came from is recorded beside what they are: `vibe.lock` package rows gain `fetched_from` (URL actually used) next to the canonical `source_url`; application run records and `steps.json` record per input the candidate that served it and the row that chose it; the install record of `vibe self` names the base used. `--json` reports carry the same fields. Nothing in a manifest or a lock is rewritten to the remapped URL, so a lock stays portable between networks and the canonical origin stays visible for review.

p.transport: Getting the first set into a closed network: `vibe remap export <package> --out <dir> [--with-artifacts]` writes a `file://` registry holding the remap package and, with `--with-artifacts`, every artifact its rows and the current project's lock name, laid out by digest; `vibe remap import <dir>` (or plain `vibe install -g --registry <dir> <package>`) installs from it, and `vibe cache import <dir>` places the artifacts into the machine store and the application download cache by their digests, verifying each. The existing `vibe registry vendor` stays the way to vendor registry packages; `export --with-artifacts` calls it.

p.commands: `vibe remap list [--json]` (active packages and local rows by layer, enabled state, policy); `explain <url|sha256> [--json]`; `test [--json]`; `enable|disable <package>`; `export`; `import`. The JSON forms are the `vibe-remap/1` documents and are the only interface a graphical client needs: a remap package shows as an installed package with a switch, `explain` answers a hover, `test` fills a readiness panel, and the provenance fields of a run record show which row served each download of an installation.

p.acceptance: Public Linux fixtures: a remap package with one row of each key installed into a scratch home, a registry package resolved through a `prefix` row to a `file://` mirror with the lock recording `fetched_from`; an application `sources` input served by a `sha256` row from a directory, the same input refused by a `deny` row with the row named; a `scope.step` row applying to one step and not another; `unmatched = "deny"` refusing an unlisted URL before any connection (the test server counts zero hits); `explain` listing two competing rows in the right order; `export --with-artifacts` then `import` and `cache import` into a second scratch home followed by an `--offline` install that succeeds; a remapped `vibe self bootstrap --release-base` accepted. MT-07 on a host with networking cut: install an application and update vibe through a remap package served from a directory.

p.decisions: Decision: remaps are data rows keyed by digest, package, registry or prefix, carried by an installable package, resolved at one point, verified by the unchanged digests. Why: digests already exist for everything fetched; a package is the one unit vibe already versions, hashes, publishes, installs and lists, so sharing and the graphical client come for free. Rejected: environment variables per host (they cannot be shared or reviewed and they leak); rewriting URLs inside manifests or locks (loses provenance, breaks portability between networks); a fallback that accepts a mirror's different bytes (the Nix lesson, and R-027); a remap package that other packages may depend on (policy belongs to the user and the project, never to a dependency). Open for the owner: whether `[proxy]` belongs in a remap package as well as in settings, and whether a project may forbid user-home packages from applying (`[remap] project_only = true`).
